nameStory: The 'rough-skinned' part of this sea anemone's name comes from its distinctive bumpy, textured surface that feels gritty to the touch - quite different from the smooth, slippery feel of many shallow-water anemones. This sandpaper-like texture helps distinguish it from its smoother cousins and gives it an almost prehistoric appearance.
description: The Rough-skinned Sea Anemone is a deep-sea creature that looks like an underwater flower with a chunky, cylindrical body topped by a crown of tentacles. Unlike the colorful anemones you might see in tide pools, this species has a more muted appearance and a distinctively bumpy, textured surface. It's built for life in the deep, cold waters far below where most divers venture. These anemones can grow to several inches across, though exact sizes vary with age and conditions.

idTips.label: Rough texture
idTips.description: The body wall feels distinctly gritty and bumpy, like fine sandpaper - completely different from the smooth, squishy texture of shallow-water anemones

idTips.label: Deep-water habitat
idTips.description: Found only in very deep water, from the continental shelf down to abyssal depths - never in tide pools or shallow areas

idTips.label: Cylindrical body
idTips.description: Has a sturdy, column-like body that feels firm rather than squishy when gently touched

idTips.label: Tentacle crown
idTips.description: Ring of tentacles around the mouth opening at the top, usually retracted when disturbed or out of water

idTips.label: Muted coloration
idTips.description: Typically brownish, grayish, or dull-colored rather than the bright reds, greens, or purples of shallow-water species

habitat: This is strictly a deep-water species found on the continental shelf and deeper ocean floors off the New England coast. You'd only encounter one if you're involved in deep-sea research, commercial fishing operations that bring up specimens from great depths, or examining scientific collections. It lives on muddy or sandy bottoms in the cold, dark waters far below the surface.

seasonality.spring: Deep-sea specimens may be brought up by research vessels or fishing operations, though the anemone experiences no seasonal changes in its stable deep-water environment.
seasonality.summer: Most likely time to encounter specimens through marine research activities or fishing bycatch, as this is peak season for deep-water operations.
seasonality.fall: Continued research activities may yield specimens, but the anemone itself experiences constant conditions in the deep sea regardless of surface seasons.
seasonality.winter: Least likely time to encounter due to reduced marine research activity, though the species remains active year-round in deep waters.

funFact: This anemone lives in one of Earth's most extreme environments - the deep sea - where the pressure can be over 100 times greater than at sea level, yet it thrives in this crushing darkness that would instantly kill most surface creatures!
confusionNotes: Since this is a deep-water species, confusion with tide pool anemones is unlikely - if you're finding it in shallow water, it's probably a different species entirely. The rough, gritty texture is the dead giveaway that distinguishes it from any smooth-bodied anemones you might encounter.
contextualKnowledge: Many people think of sea anemones as colorful tide pool creatures, but the vast majority of anemone species actually live in the deep sea where we rarely see them. This species represents the hidden diversity of anemones that most people never encounter.
compareHints: Since this is the only Actinostola species recorded in New England waters, compare it to other deep-sea anemones by focusing on that distinctive rough, sandpaper-like texture. Most other deep-water anemone species have smooth body walls, making the rough skin a reliable identifying feature. The firm, cylindrical body shape also differs from the more blob-like or elongated forms of other deep-sea anemone families.
